blocked.name: Mother sauces
blocking: Bearnaise and avgolemono make opposite claims about the same variable. Bearnaise `break`: 'the extra acid buys it slightly more room than hollandaise'. Avgolemono `break`: 'the acid makes it curdle sooner than allemande would'. Acid cannot both raise and lower the ceiling in one family. The true difference in the avgolemono case is starch, not acid: allemande has a roux, and starch granules physically interfere with yolk proteins aggregating, which is why a floured egg sauce tolerates more heat. Fix both: avgolemono -> 'no starch to keep the yolks apart, so it curdles sooner than allemande'; bearnaise -> drop the acid claim and use something true and specific, e.g. 'the same ceiling as hollandaise - the reduction replaces the water, not the limit'.

The standfirst dates the five-sauce list to the nineteenth century. It is not: Careme's list (1833) was four and included allemande; Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire is 1903, and hollandaise appears among the basic sauces only in the 1907 English edition, which is the origin of the modern five. Since the whole page's argument is that the number is a decision made at a date, the date should be right. Suggested: 'Five sauces that a French kitchen settled on in 1903, and four sauces from elsewhere that answer the same question without it.'

'On the count of five' has the arithmetic wrong: 'put hollandaise and tomate in the empty slots' implies two slots were vacated when only allemande's was (four minus one plus two equals five - one slot vacated, one newly created). It also compresses the sequence. Rewrite along the lines of: 'Escoffier kept the first three, demoted allemande to a veloute derivative because it is one, promoted tomate, and added hollandaise - four became five, and the fifth slot is one he made.'

Three region chips are two things joined by 'and', which is exactly what breaks the 'By region' nesting: avgolemono has 'Greece and Turkey' plus a chip that literally begins 'and the Sephardi kitchen', and gumbo has 'Cajun and Creole'. Split them into separate chips - ['Eastern Mediterranean', 'Greece', 'Turkey', 'the Sephardi kitchen'] and ['United States', 'Louisiana', 'Cajun', 'Creole'] - and never start a chip with 'and'.

Ankake `break` third chip, 'clouds and slumps as it cools', is wrong for one of the two starches the `thicken` cell names. Kudzu sets on cooling - it is the starch used to make kuzumochi and gomadofu, i.e. it gels cold rather than slumping. Either scope the chip to potato starch ('potato starch loses its gloss as it cools') or replace it with a failure both starches share.

Espagnole is the only dish whose `break` cell says nothing about breaking: after the leading 'safe at a hard boil', the two sub-chips ('thickens far less than a pale roux of the same weight', 'so it takes a great deal more of it') are thickening power, which already lives in the `thicken` facet and in the note 'On how far you cook the flour'. Replace with actual failure modes, e.g. 'bitter for good if the roux catches' and 'greasy unless it is skimmed as it simmers' - the latter also sets up demi-glace's skimming chip.

Bechamel's region chip 'claimed by Tuscany as well' states a disputed legend as fact and is narrower than the claim actually is. The Italian claim runs through Catherine de' Medici and salsa colla, and archival work finds no Italian chefs among her servants from her arrival in France to her death. Either drop the chip or make the status visible: 'Italy claims it too, on a Medici story the archives do not support'.

Bearnaise's note says the sauce 'has nothing to do with Bearn'. It has an indirect but real link: it was made at Le Pavillon Henri IV, in the former residence of Henry IV, who was from Bearn - the name honours the king, not the province's cooking. Rewrite as: 'named not for its cooking but for Henry IV le Bearnais, whose old residence housed the restaurant where it was made, twenty kilometres from Paris and seven hundred from Bearn.'
reasons: Check 1 (distinctness) passes: all 16 rows differ. The tightest pair is Bechamel/Mornay, which differ in `add` and `break`; Espagnole/Demi-glace differ in liquid, add and break; Hollandaise/Bearnaise differ in liquid and add. No row is written twice.

Check 2 (dead dimensions) passes. `region` looks French-heavy but splits five ways (France / United States / Eastern Mediterranean / Japan / Mexico); `break` splits five ways and is the most load-bearing column on the page; `add` has six dishes at 'nothing but seasoning' but that is a real bucket, not a constant.

Check 4 (leading chips) passes almost everywhere: `thicken` leads with 'a roux' for all seven roux sauces before naming the colour, `break` leads with the boil/simmer/splits verdict, and `liquid` leads with milk / white stock / brown stock, so the fork lands on the shared move. Allemande grouping under 'a roux' while avgolemono groups under 'a liaison' is a deliberate split and the notes defend it.

Check 5 (parent) passes. Mornay and Soubise under Bechamel, Supreme and Allemande under Veloute, Demi-glace under Espagnole, Bordelaise under Demi-glace, Bearnaise under Hollandaise are all genuine base-plus-one-thing relationships; the four non-French sauces are correctly parentless with an explicit argument in 'On depth'.

Check 6 (parochialism): acceptable but thin. Twelve of sixteen are French, which the standfirst and 'On the count of five' honestly own, and the four outsiders each carry a different mechanism (dark roux, egg alone, bare starch, ground seed). Non-blocking suggestion: one more entry would close an obvious gap - a yogurt/nut-paste gravy (korma type, cashew or almond paste plus yogurt, which splits if the yogurt boils unstabilised) adds a thickener the page lacks and a `break` value nothing else occupies.

Check 7 (facts) mostly holds up. Verified sound: Careme's four (espagnole, veloute, allemande, bechamel, 1833); Escoffier demoting allemande ('Allemande Sauce is not, strictly speaking, a basic sauce'); bearnaise invented by Collinet at Le Pavillon Henri IV, Saint-Germain-en-Laye, 1836; pipian from Nahuatl and associated with Puebla and Oaxaca; demi-glace as espagnole plus an equal measure of stock reduced by half, Madeira finish, jellies cold; katakuriko thinning back out if held hot. Corrections are in blocking.

Check 8 (standfirst): the shape is right - it states the editorial claim, names the mechanism ('flour cooked in fat, an egg yolk, a starch, a ground seed') and explains why derivatives are drawn underneath, with no food-praise. Only its dating is wrong (see blocking).

Non-blocking nits worth a pass: avgolemono's 'no fat and no flour at all' should be 'no added fat' (yolk is roughly a third fat, and the page elsewhere trades on exactly that); ankake's `add` cell is three parallel ingredients (soy sauce / mirin / grated ginger) rather than a headline plus refinements, unlike every other cell on the page; sauce tomate's 'Provence' looks like Escoffier's own birthplace rather than the sauce's, and 'France' alone would be safer; 'Gumbo roux' is the only entry named for a component rather than a sauce, which is honest but inconsistent with its neighbours.

blocked.name: Aromatic base
blocking: Holy trinity's `heat` cell leads with "added to fat already browned", which describes the fat, not the vegetables — and that state is already recorded in its `fat` cell as "thickened into a roux with flour". The trinity's vegetables are softened, never coloured. Two readings pay for it: in "By how far it is cooked" the trinity becomes a top-level branch of one that answers a question the column didn't ask; and in "By what the knife does" its departure from the pale group leaves Mirepoix and Soffritto alone there, so grow() treats their second chips as refinements, skips them, and bottoms both out as two unlabelled leaves under "diced with a knife > kept pale > onion > carrot > celery" with nothing separating them — in the reading about the knife, while "cut finer than a mirepoix" sits unused in soffritto's cell. Fix: heat: ["kept pale", "added to fat already browned", "the roux taken to peanut or chocolate first", "the vegetables stop the roux cooking"]. I simulated it: all three readings then fork cleanly and no two dishes share a leaf.

Sofrito contradicts its own note. Its aromatics are onion, garlic, culantro, ají dulce, cubanelle — no tomato — and the note ends "Without tomato it is recaíto", so the row as written is recaíto, not sofrito. Pick one: add "tomato" to the aromatics chips (and then reconsider "kept green" in heat), or rewrite the last sentence to own the green version — e.g. "This is the green one, recaíto, named for the recao — culantro — that makes it; put tomato in and it is sofrito proper."

Tarka's note misattributes a regional name: "Also called tadka in the west, chhaunk in the north, baghar in the Deccan, phoron in Bengal". Tadka is not a western term — it is the same Hindi word as tarka, used in the same north/central belt as chhaunk. The western names are vaghar (Gujarati) and phodni (Marathi). Suggested replacement keeping the count: "Also called tadka or chhaunk in the north, vaghar in Gujarat, phodni in Maharashtra, baghar in the Deccan, phoron in Bengal — one move, five names."

The standfirst's "The vegetables barely vary — an onion and two friends" is false for a third of its own table and is contradicted by the family's own note ("the base looks nothing like the European one and does exactly the same job"). Suppengrün has no onion, epis leads on scallion and herbs, ginger and scallion has no onion, krueng gaeng is stems and roots, and tarka has no vegetable at all. Qualify it to the entries it describes — e.g. "In Europe the vegetables barely vary — an onion and two friends — but what a kitchen does to them..." — so the opening claim survives contact with the rest of the family.
reasons: Check 1 passes: all 16 rows are distinct across the five dimensions — I ran the same signature test the build script uses (data/canon/aromatic-base.json, verified against scripts/build-canon.mjs), no collisions.

Check 2 passes on the constant test — every dimension varies — but `fat` never actually forks anything in any of the three readings: I grew all three trees and no fat chip appears as a label in any of them. It is carried in the table and never in a tree. Cheapest fix, if you want it working: make the second nesting ["form","heat","fat"] instead of ["form","heat","aromatics"]. That also kills the ladder the current order draws — "diced with a knife > kept pale > onion > carrot > celery", three nested labels with one branch each — and gives butter-vs-olive-oil as the mirepoix/soffritto fork, which is a better answer than either of their second heat chips.

Check 3 passes: no chip is two things joined. The eight chips containing "and" ("lifted out and thrown away", "hardest thing first and softest last", "loosened with vinegar and sour orange") are each one move, and the style matches the rest of the corpus (chilli-condiment.json does the same).

Check 5: `parent` is absent throughout and that is the right call here. The two relationships that look like descent both run through an ancestor that is not in the table — Castilian sofrito is only mentioned inside sofregit's note, and the trinity's parentage is contested between mirepoix and Spanish sofrito, so a single parent link would be an overclaim. This matches the position sausage.json argues explicitly.

Check 6 passes: 5 of 16 rows are European and the rest span the Caribbean, Mexico, Brazil, Iran, China, India (2), Nigeria, Thailand and Ethiopia. Gaps if it ever grows: no Levantine or Arab base, nothing Vietnamese or Indonesian, no Cuban or Dominican sofrito.

Check 7, things I checked and believe are right: mirepoix 2:1:1 by weight; battuto as the raw mix and soffriggere as "under-fry"; the Suppengrün bundle; roux taken to peanut or chocolate with the trinity added cold to arrest it; picada closing what sofregit opens; ata lilo / ata din din, tatashe for colour and ata rodo for heat; bào xiāng; piaz dagh as "hot onion"; niter kibbeh added after the dry pan; recaíto named for recao.

Naming, worth a disambiguating clause rather than a rewrite: this feature already ships a curry-paste family containing "Kroeung" (Cambodia) and "Recado rojo" (Yucatán). "Krueng gaeng" and "Recaudo" here are different things with near-identical names, and neither note tells the reader so. "Krueng gaeng" is also an informal romanization — khrueang gaeng, or the everyday phrik gaeng, would be steadier. And "recaudo" for this base is regional Mexican usage (the cited source is a family blog); the note never says the name varies while the technique doesn't.

Minor consistency: the region chip "the north" (Bhuna masala) is unique to this file — curry-paste.json and frozen-dessert.json both write "North India" for the same place. It never renders today (the tree treats it as a refinement and skips it), so this is housekeeping.

Minor: Tarka's form cell is "left whole" then "nothing chopped at all", which restates rather than adds a second decision. And the "On the oil coming back" note covers the same ground as curry-paste's "On frying the paste" (bhuna plus cracked coconut cream); obe ata is the new example, so it earns its place, but pecah minyak probably belongs in only one of the two.
Check 8: the standfirst does work rather than praise — it names the four decisions and they map onto four of the five facets — but one clause in it is not true of this table; see blocking.

Edits go in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/aromatic-base.json, then `node scripts/build-canon.mjs` to regenerate src/data/canon-families.ts. I checked the four fixes below against the validator — all pass.

blocked.name: Curry paste
blocking: Line 508, the 'On the word curry' note is falsified by the table: it says 'the roux is the only dish nested under another', but Panang paste is also nested (parent: Red curry paste), and the Panang note itself says so. Rewrite as e.g. 'only two dishes here are nested under another, and this is one of them' — or drop the clause and keep the point about the powder-and-roux being a small family inside this one.

Lines 421 and 447: Curry powder and Curry roux carry chilli chip ['mild dried chilli']. That leads with an unshared value, so in the 'By chilli' nesting these two fork away into their own branch and never join the dried-chilli group they belong to — the fresh/dried/none decision the family is built on is not drawn for them. Change both to ['dried chilli', 'mild']. The second chip then sits alongside 'soaked soft', 'soaked in the vinegar', 'roasted dry' and 'sun-dried then roasted' as the treatment fork, which is exactly what those slots are for.

Line 239: Bumbu's spice cell is ['coriander seed ground in raw'] — a single chip carrying both the treatment and the seed, and leading with neither the shared move nor a value any sibling has. Every other dish leads with a treatment chip ('whole seeds toasted first', 'whole seeds ground raw', 'no dry spice at all'). Change to ['whole seeds ground raw', 'coriander seed'] so Bumbu forks with Unroasted curry powder and British curry powder. As it stands the raw-versus-toasted decision that the 'On toasting' note calls the argument is invisible for Bumbu in every reading.

Lines 261 and 289: Vindaloo's ['pounded to a wet paste', 'let down with palm vinegar'] and Recado rojo's ['pounded to a wet paste', 'let down with sour orange juice'] each name their own acid in the fork slot, so the tree splits them into two singleton branches. The Recado note explicitly claims these are the same move independently arrived at ('acid plus a pounded base is what you do when there is no refrigeration'), and the tree cannot draw the claim. Insert the shared move first: ['pounded to a wet paste', 'let down with acid', 'palm vinegar'] and ['pounded to a wet paste', 'let down with acid', 'sour orange juice'].

Backbone for Green curry paste, Red curry paste and Panang paste omits garlic and shallot, which are standard in both pastes (kratiem and hom daeng), while Kroeung, Rempah and Bumbu all list them. That makes garlic and shallot read as distinguishing chips when all six share them, and it puts the table in direct conflict with the Kroeung note, which says kroeung is 'the Thai aromatics without the chilli and without the seeds' — as written, kroeung's aromatics are not the Thai ones. Preferred fix: add 'garlic' and 'shallot' to the three Thai rows (and 'garlic' to Massaman, which already lists shallot); then Kroeung's real distinguishing chips are fresh turmeric root and makrut lime leaf, and the note becomes true. The alternative — dropping garlic and shallot from the Southeast Asian rows — loses less true information but leaves the note unsupported.
reasons: Reviewed against the on-disk file /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/curry-paste.json, which is identical to the JSON supplied (16 dishes, not 15).

Check 1 passes: all 16 rows are distinct. The closest pairs are Red vs Green (chilli), Red vs Panang (backbone gains roasted peanut), Roasted vs Unroasted Sri Lankan (spice treatment) and Curry powder vs Curry roux (form gains the roux) — each is a genuine one-decision difference, which is the point of the family.

Check 2 passes: no dead dimension. form splits 10 wet / 6 dry, chilli splits fresh / dried / none, spice splits toasted / raw / none, backbone splits stems-and-roots / seeds-only / no fresh aromatics, region has 13 values across 16 dishes.

Check 3 passes: no chip is two things joined by a comma or 'and'. 'stirred into a butter-and-flour roux' names one thing. 'sun-dried then roasted' (Berbere) is two moves in one chip — house style elsewhere splits these ('boiled' / 'then pan-fried' in the exemplar) — minor, not blocking.

Check 5 passes: parent is used twice and both are real. Panang is red plus peanuts; the roux is the powder plus a roux. It is correctly withheld from Massaman, and the Massaman note argues the withholding rather than leaving it implicit — that is the family working as designed.

Check 6 passes: Thailand 4 of 16 is the only concentration, and the rest run Cambodia, Malaysia, Indonesia, Goa, Tamil Nadu, North India, Sri Lanka, Britain, Japan, Yucatán, Ethiopia. The European and Caribbean fried-aromatic bases (sofrito, epis, obe ata, recaudo) live in the sibling family /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/aromatic-base.json, so their absence here is a boundary, not a gap.

Check 7 mostly passes: makrut (not the slur), belacan, terasi, prahok, pecah minyak, badapu thuna paha, korarima, besobela, carne de vinha d'alhos, naranja agria, Yucatán, karē rū all check out. Sri Lankan roasted/unroasted, the Goan palm-vinegar claim and awaze-as-let-down-berbere are right.

Check 8 passes: the standfirst names the four actual decisions (fresh or dried chilli, dry pan or not, which aromatics, wet or dry) and does not praise the food. The opening 'almost nobody cooks a curry from scratch at the stove' is a slightly slippery phrasing — making the paste IS from scratch — but the meaning, that the base is built separately and first, survives it.

Minor, non-blocking: Massaman's spice cell omits coriander and cumin seed, which most massaman pastes do contain. The omission is what makes the row look unlike red paste, and the note's historical argument doesn't depend on it — worth being a deliberate choice rather than an oversight.

Minor, non-blocking: line 462, the Curry roux note reads as if the roux arrived with the navy in the 1870s. The thickened stew did; the roux block is mid-twentieth-century. 'which arrived with the British navy in the 1870s as a thickened stew' is defensible if 'which' points at the stew, but a reader will attach it to the roux.

blocked.name: Chilli condiment
blocking: The primary reading draws one facet out of three, and `form` is never drawn in ANY reading. I ran grow() from /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts against /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/chilli-condiment.json: 'By what happens to the chilli' [method, form, add] comes out depth 2, facets drawn: method (1/3). It forks correctly on method chip 1 (pounded raw / boiled first / dried in the sun / fermented in salt / fried in oil / stirred from a dry blend), then forks again on method chip 2 — which is unique to every dish — into singletons: 'ground in a stone mortar — Sambal oelek', 'herbs and chilli in the same mortar — Zhoug', 'some houses roast the peppers first — Harissa' (a hedged optional step used as a fork label), 'hot oil poured over the flakes — Chilli oil'. The refinement guard cannot save it: it fires only when no dish in the group has a chip 3, and every method cell here has 3 or 4 chips. The cost is that `form` appears in no tree at all, so the paste/oil split the standfirst names as one of its three separators — and that the whole 'On paste and oil' note is built on — is never drawn, leaving chilli oil an undifferentiated sibling of chilli crisp, salsa macha, nam phrik phao and XO. Fix by capping `method` at two chips (shared move + one detail) and moving the rest into the dish note. Verified: with method truncated to two chips the reading becomes depth 3, facets drawn method, form (2/3), giving 'fried in oil → oil alone — Chilli oil' beside 'fried in oil → oil with solids in it → crunchy / gritty / jammy / shredded', and 'pounded raw → a paste → coarse / loose and green / dense / thick / smooth'. A second verified route, if you want to keep three chips, is to make chip 2 shared across each method group (e.g. 'never sees heat' on all five pounded-raw rows) and leave the idiosyncratic phrase at chip 3 — that also reaches `form`.

'By what else is in the jar' [add, method] flattens its largest branch: under 'garlic' — 9 of the 16 dishes — `method` is never drawn. The tree renders nine singletons labelled by their second ingredient ('coriander leaf by the bunch — Zhoug', 'blue fenugreek — Ajika', 'caraway — Harissa', 'lemon — Shatta', 'fried soybeans — Chilli crisp', 'peanuts — Salsa macha', 'shallots — Nam phrik phao', 'dried scallop — XO sauce', 'ginger — Awaze'). That is a list of chip labels, not a second reading — the same failure that blocked sausage's 'By grind'. Two verified fixes: (a) cap `add` at two chips for the garlic group, which makes it fork garlic → pounded raw {Zhoug, Ajika, Harissa} / fermented in salt — Shatta / fried in oil {Chilli crisp, Salsa macha, Nam phrik phao, XO sauce} / stirred from a dry blend — Awaze, at the cost of moving caraway, dried scallop and Jinhua ham into the notes; or (b) insert a shared category chip at index 1 ('a herb' / 'a spice' / 'an acid' / 'a nut' / 'dried seafood') before the specific ingredients, which I tested and which at least replaces nine singletons with real groups (a spice: Ajika, Harissa, Awaze; a nut: Chilli crisp, Salsa macha; dried seafood: Nam phrik phao, XO sauce) — though it still does not reach `method`.

The standfirst, the root and the 'On the four ways' note each count differently, and none of the counts matches the table. (a) 'Every one of these is the same fruit made to keep' is contradicted by two of its own rows: awaze's form cell reads 'made fresh each time · days' and its note says the preserving was done before the condiment was; zhoug's reads 'a week or two' and its note says it will not keep. (b) 'What separates them is which of those four things you do' — the table has six method leads, and neither ají amarillo paste (boiled, then frozen) nor awaze (stirred from a dry blend) is any of the four. (c) The root, 'Chilli · salt · and one way of stopping it spoiling — oil, a ferment, or the sun', omits salt alone, which is precisely ajika's point ('salt is the only preservative', 'keeps a year'). (d) The note titled 'On the four ways to keep it' names a different four — salt, oil, acid, fermentation — then adds a fifth two sentences later ('Biber salçası simply removes the water'). Pick one honest count and make all four statements agree: either say five or six ways and name them, or say 'most of them' and let awaze and ají amarillo be the stated exceptions.

Chilli oil's `add` cell breaks check 3 and renders as a fork label. The cell is ['nothing else', 'sometimes cassia and star anise steeped in the oil'] — two ingredients and a hedge joined into one chip, sitting under a lead chip that says there is nothing else; in 'By what else is in the jar' it draws as a branch of 'nothing else' beside 'salt'. Change the cell to ['nothing else', 'salt'] and put the whole spices in the dish note ('some versions steep cassia and star anise in the oil'). This also improves the tree — chilli oil then joins the salt group with sambal oelek, ají amarillo, biber salçası and crema di peperoncino instead of hanging off its own branch.

Gochujang factual fix: 'aged in onggi jars on the roof'. Traditionally the jangdok/onggi stand on the jangdokdae, a raised stone platform in the yard sited for sun — the roof is the modern apartment substitute, not the tradition the chip is describing. Change the chip to 'aged in onggi on the jangdokdae' (or '…on the sunlit platform in the yard'). The note's mechanism is right and worth keeping: malt enzymes saccharify the cooked rice starch while the meju culture works on the protein.
reasons: Checks 1, 2 and 5 pass cleanly. No two rows are identical (all 16 differ on method alone); no column is constant — `form` splits 11 paste / 1 oil alone / 4 oil-with-solids, `add` splits 5 / 9 / 2, `method` into six leads; no empty cells, no repeated chips inside a cell. `parent` is used exactly once, for the one claim that is real (chilli crisp is la you with the frying left in), and correctly withheld from the two convergence pairs (sambal oelek / crema di peperoncino, chilli crisp / salsa macha), which the 'On depth' note explains rather than asserts.

Check 6 passes: 14 countries across four continents (Java, Yemen, Abkhazia, Peru, Tunisia, Hatay, Palestine, Pixian, Korea, Guizhou, Veracruz, Thailand, Hong Kong, Calabria, Ethiopia). Nothing parochial. If it ever grows, the one gap that shows is West Africa — Ghanaian shito is a fried chilli-and-dried-fish oil that would sit exactly beside XO sauce and nam phrik phao, and a Malay sambal belacan would give the fried-shrimp-paste line a second point.

Check 7 (facts) mostly holds up. Verified against sources: XO sauce — 1980s, The Peninsula in Tsim Sha Tsui (Spring Moon), no cognac in it; ajika is Abkhaz for salt, utskho suneli is blue fenugreek, and the Abkhaz/Megrelian versions are tomato-free; harissa's baklouti and caraway; acı/tatlı biber salçası; the ají amarillo blanch-in-changed-water. Salsa macha's history checks out too — Totonac dry ground chilli-and-seed pastes in the Orizaba/Córdoba/Zongolica highlands, oil arriving with the Spanish — though the Wikipedia source cited says none of it (it offers only macha < macho or machacada), so that note is running ahead of its footnote.

Two smaller wording problems in the notes. (a) Sambal oelek: 'The name is the tool, not the chilli — oelek is the grinding done in a cobek with a stone pestle' contradicts itself inside one sentence. Ulek is the action (the cobek is the mortar, the ulekan the pestle) — either 'the name is the method' or 'the name is the pestle', not tool-then-action. (b) 'On the ones next door': 'piri-piri is the same idea with lemon, Tabasco is that plus three years in oak' reads as though Tabasco is lemony — it is a salt-fermented mash aged three years and then cut with vinegar.

The `chilli` column — the one the family is named for — is inert. It appears in no nesting, and because keyChips() is computed against nesting 0 in the table, it marks zero key chips in all three readings (method 52/52 chips marked, chilli 0/30, add 0/56, form 0/64). Its lead vocabulary is also unnormalised: 12 distinct lead values over 16 rows, with 'dried chilli', 'dried chillies' and 'dried red chillies' as three spellings of one idea. Normalising the lead chip to fresh / dried / already ground would cost nothing and would let a fourth reading ('By the chilli') exist — worth doing, though I am not blocking on it.

The `region` column mixes three conventions: broad→narrow (Indonesia · Java; Turkey · Hatay; China · Sichuan · Pixian; Mexico · Veracruz; Italy · Calabria), narrow→broad (Abkhazia · Georgia; Palestine · Levant), and peer-country pairs meaning 'also eaten here' (Yemen · Israel; Ethiopia · Eritrea). Only the first kind can ever group siblings. Worth settling on one meaning for chip 2, with Abkhazia probably left standing alone rather than filed under Georgia.

Minor, non-blocking: awaze states the same fact twice across two columns ('berbere loosened with tej or wine' in method, 'tej or wine to loosen it' in add); biber salçası's chilli chip 'hot for acı and mild for tatlı' packs two products into one chip (harmless only because `chilli` never forks anything); doubanjiang's 'the two married and aged in open crocks' and biber salçası's 'ground then spread on trays' are each two moves in one chip — all three disappear if you act on blocking item 1.

blocked.name: Dip
blocking: Standfirst's closing line is false by the family's own chips. "Change nothing about burnt aubergine except the fat you beat into it and you have left Beirut for Tehran" — but Kashk-e bademjan's base chip says the aubergine is "fried in oil until gold", not burnt, and its acid changes too (lemon to fermented whey). Three decisions move, not one. Either name the two that matter (the aubergine is fried instead of burnt and the sour arrives as kashk) or pick a pair that really does turn on one move.

Root line excludes four of its own members. "broken down with salt and garlic" — guacamole, taramasalata and tirokafteri have no garlic. "slackened with a fat" — Nam phrik num's own fat cell reads "no fat at all", and its note celebrates exactly that. "eaten cold" — Ful medames is a hot breakfast. "with bread" — nam phrik num goes with sticky rice (its own body chip says so), coconut chutney with idli and dosa, guacamole with tortilla. Loosen it, e.g. "Something soft or softened · broken down with salt in a mortar or a machine · usually carried by a fat and cut by something sour · scooped at room temperature with bread or rice". The same bread-only framing recurs in the "On what is not here" note ("holds a piece of bread up") and should move with it.

Muhammara's region cell leads "Syria" while every other Levantine dish leads "Levant". Under the "By region" nesting this forks Aleppo away from Tahini sauce, Hummus, Mutabbal and Baba ganoush into a sibling branch of its own — the tree cannot fork on a shared move that is not there. Change to ["Levant", "Syria", "Aleppo"].

Coconut chutney's note claims "The only one whose last move happens in a hot pan after the grinding is done", contradicted inside the same file by Kashk-e bademjan's fat chip "dried mint bloomed in more oil and poured over" (na'na dagh is precisely that move, after the pounding) and by Ajvar's "a last film on top to seal the jar". Narrow it — what is actually singular is that the tempering is the seasoning rather than a garnish, or that the fat arrives only at the end and only hot.

Taramasalata's note makes two claims the file contradicts. "the only one that is a true emulsion": Skordalia's own fat chip says the oil is "worked in a thread at a time like mayonnaise", and the "On what tahini does" note opens by calling sesame paste an emulsion. "The only savoury base here that was preserved before it was pulped": feta is a brined, preserved, savoury base, and Tirokafteri's acid cell leads with the brine it was kept in. Narrow both — e.g. the only base that is cured fish, and the only one where the base does the emulsifying the way a yolk does.

Tzatziki's note says "The only base here that arrived already sour", contradicted by feta in Tirokafteri, which is lactic-soured and whose acid cell leads with the brine it came in rather than anything poured in. Tzatziki's own chip also admits "a spoonful of vinegar in some houses", so the "nothing needs pouring in" half is hedged already. Rewrite to what is actually true and singular: the sourness is the base's own and the whole technique is wringing the cucumber. The same claim recurs in "On the four decisions" ("in tzatziki nothing added because the base soured itself") — fix both, and consider making Tirokafteri's acid lead "the cheese's own souring" with the brine as the second chip, so the two sit together where they belong.

Guacamole's note claims "the only base that is neither cooked nor cured nor fermented, and the only one that brings its own fat in the flesh". Fresh coconut, grated off the shell, is raw; and both Muhammara and Coconut chutney lead their fat cell with "the nut's own oil". What is actually unique is the conjunction: it is the only one that goes in raw AND has nothing poured in at all (coconut chutney pours over its tempering oil, muhammara works in olive oil). Say that instead.

"On what tahini does" gets the mechanism wrong, and it is presented as chemistry. Tahini seizes when any aqueous liquid enters the fat-continuous paste — plain water does it identically — as the emulsion inverts; it is not that "the acid drops the pH and the protein grabs the water". Lemon juice seizes it because it is mostly water. The paling likewise comes from water dispersed through the paste, not from acid. Rewrite so the sequence (seize, then let down with cold water, ending paler and thicker) stays but the cause is right. While there, resolve the clash with "On the mortar and the machine", which asserts "The blender is the only one that changes colour as well as texture" while this note has hummus turning white by chemistry rather than by tool.
